newsitem.title: UK: British pipeline inflation pressures plunge.
newsitem.headline: British pipeline inflation pressures plunge.

text.p: British pipeline inflation pressures fell back spectacularly in November, with input prices dropping 3.2 percent from the previous month, the sharpest fall since 1985, official figures showed on Monday.

Input prices, which reflect prices of raw materials bought in by British manufacturers, were depressed by the pound's meteoric rise over the past four months, the Office for National Statistics said. They were down 5.5 percent from a year earlier.
Output prices, a measure of prices leaving the factory gate, were unchanged on the month and only 2.1 percent higher year-on-year.
The government welcomed the figures as heralding favourable retail price inflation data to come.
"Today's low inflation at the factory gate is tomorrow's good news for prices in the shops," said Angela Knight, economic secretary to the Treasury.

But City economists were less confident that underlying retail price inflation, which jumped unexpectedly to an annual rate of 3.3 percent in October, would necessarily follow the trend in producer prices.
They noted that retailers had been increasing their profit margins, which were battered during Britain's recent economic slowdown, in the face of steadily rising consumer demand.

"We should see output price inflation contained over the next few months, but I would be a little more hesitant to extend that to the retail price level," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.
November underlying inflation figures, due on Thursday, are expected to hold steady at 3.3 percent, well above the government's medium-term target of 2.5 percent
The ONS said the 0.8 percent annual rise in core output prices, which exclude food, drink, tobacco and petroleum prices, was the lowest in nearly 30 years.
"The recent strength of sterling is clearly working to keep raw material costs under tight control right across the board," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Measured against a basket of other major currencies, the pound has leapt more than 10 percent since early August. Prior to a tumble last week, the currency had gained about 12 percent.
British manufacturers rely on imports for most of their raw materials and a stronger pound reduces import costs.

The figures will be welcome news for Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke ahead of his monthly meeting on monetary policy with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
The Bank has cited mounting inflationary pressures to justify a call for interest rates to be raised from the present 6.0 percent.
Clarke, who raised rates by a quarter of one percent in October, will be keen to avoid further increases before the general election, due by next May.
"The producer price figures were excellent figures and very useful ammunition for Mr Clarke in the interest rate debate," Loynes said.

A Reuter poll of 21 London-based economists found not one expecting base rates to be raised from six percent this week even though they were all caught out when Clarke allowed a quarter-point rate rise in October.
Loynes said benign background inflation should lead to lower retail prices in due course.
"The steep drop in core output price inflation should... allow inflation to fall next year even as retailers widen their margins to take advantage of stronger high street activity."
